findings.committee: Executive
findings.headline: Special educational needs statements growing 10% annually despite management action; council building 152 new local provision places from January 2027
findings.detail: EHCP (Education, Health and Care Plan) statements continue growing at 10% year-on-year despite new guidance and management efforts to slow increase. Director attributes this to national drivers (415% increase since Children and Family Act) and local factors (43% tribunal increase). Council is responding by building 152 satellite unit places within local schools to reduce reliance on expensive out-of-borough provision.
findings.matters: SEN growth is a major budget driver for all councils; building in-borough provision rather than purchasing external placements at £10-30k per pupil directly affects cost trajectory and budget sustainability.
findings.figures: 10% year-on-year EHCP growth; 415% national increase since Children and Family Act; 43% tribunal increase; 152 satellite unit places planned; first 100 by January 2027
findings.quote: Since the Children and Family Act there has been a quadrupling in increase – 415% increase nationally and a 43% increase in Tribunals. The new capacity within the borough will deliver 152 new placements through these satellite units with the first 100 places being available in January 2027 and the remaining 52 in phase 2.

findings.headline: Schools funding deficit estimated £57.5m with government offering up to 90% relief if council meets reform conditions

findings.matters: DSG deficits held separately from General Fund represent substantial obligations that can affect overall budget resilience; government relief availability significantly impacts medium-term financial outlook.

findings.headline: Interest income outperformance of £2.0m is one-off, driven by High Needs Stability Grant announced after budget-setting

findings.quote: The Plan anticipates that the reform programme will contribute to a £12.52m High Needs budget cost reduction by 2029/30, alongside a £1.67m reduction in SEN Transport expenditure by 2029/30. These projections are dependent on successful delivery of the Experts at Hand model, workforce expansion, local sufficiency and inclusion base development, and continued partner commitment to earlier intervention and shared accountability.

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Annex A - The Local SEND Reform Plan
findings.headline: Workforce capacity and recruitment constraints rated as Critical/Likely risk to plan delivery, with national shortages and local competition limiting specialist staff supply
findings.detail: The partnership has identified workforce capacity as a Critical-rated risk with Likely likelihood, threatening the ability to recruit and retain sufficient specialist and support staff at scale across speech and language therapy, occupational therapy, educational psychology and specialist teaching. Mitigations include joint commissioning between LA and ICB and exploration of reciprocal arrangements with other areas, but supply-side constraints are noted as systemic.
findings.matters: Workforce cost inflation and recruitment difficulty are live pressures in many councils' SEND systems; a plan-critical risk rated Critical/Likely suggests the savings pathway is contingent on outcomes outside the council's direct control, materially affecting delivery probability.
findings.figures: Critical/Likely RAG rating; national workforce shortages explicitly cited as constraint
findings.quote: Risk that national workforce shortages and local competition limit the ability to recruit and retain sufficient specialist and support staff to deliver the reform programme at scale.

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Annex A - The Local SEND Reform Plan
findings.headline: £2.66m Experts at Hand investment in year 1 (2026/27), with >80% (£2.13m) deployed to frontline clinical and specialist staff delivery
findings.detail: The plan directs £2,664,902 to launch the Experts at Hand early intervention model in its first year, with majority funding (>£2.1m) allocated to frontline workforce including specialist teachers, speech and language therapists, occupational therapists and educational psychologists. Remaining <10% each for transformation activity and programme administration. This represents material new recurrent investment to drive the projected savings.
findings.matters: The funding model and allocation show whether the council is investing adequately to achieve stated savings, and whether transformation is properly resourced; underinvestment in frontline delivery would undermine the entire savings plan's credibility.
findings.figures: Total EAH allocation £2,664,902; direct delivery £2,132,433 (>80%); transformation £266,490 (<10%); administration £265,979 (<10%)
findings.quote: Total EAH allocation Total funding allocated to the Experts at Hand model £ 2,664,902 100% Direct delivery Frontline workforce including Specialist Teachers, SaLT, OT, EP and associated delivery staff £2,132,433 >80%

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Annex A - The Local SEND Reform Plan
findings.headline: EHCP caseload growth projected to moderate from 4,784 (2025) to 5,633 by 2029, with growth rate slowing from 2028
findings.detail: Current demand for statutory assessment remains high at 1,065 EHC needs assessment requests and 756 plans issued annually. The plan projects total EHCP growth of 849 over four years (17.7%), but projects the rate to decelerate from 2028, suggesting earlier intervention is expected to suppress future demand growth. Demand management is central to the £14.19m savings pathway.
findings.matters: Demand trajectory directly drives high needs expenditure and determines whether cost reductions are sustainable; a council successfully moderating demand growth demonstrates system-level reform traction, whereas acceleration would signal reform plan failure.
findings.figures: 4,784 EHCPs (December 2025); 5,633 projected by 2029; 1,065 annual assessment requests; 756 plans issued annually
findings.quote: Demand for SEND support has grown significantly, with 4,784 children and young people with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) in 2025, placing sustained pressure on mainstream inclusion, specialist sufficiency, workforce capacity and the financial sustainability of the high needs system.

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Annex A - The Local SEND Reform Plan
findings.headline: 435 pupils placed in expensive independent and non-maintained specialist settings, creating sustained high-cost pressure that plan aims to reduce from 2028
findings.detail: Bromley has higher proportion of independent placements (7% of EHCP cohort) than national and London averages (5%), with over 400 children placed in these settings often outside the borough. This drives material cost pressure on the high needs block and generates additional transport costs. The reform strategy focuses on expanding local provision to reduce reliance on these placements from 2028 onwards.
findings.matters: Independent placements are high-unit-cost drivers of high needs pressure; the scale of this cohort (435 pupils) and the plan's timeline for reduction are directly material to understanding whether the council's cost pressures are being actively managed or are structural.
findings.figures: 435 children and young people placed in NMSS or independent provision; 7% of EHCP cohort vs 5% national/London average; over 400 out-of-borough placements
findings.quote: Over 400 children are placed in these settings, often outside the borough, increasing transport and placement costs. Our strategy focuses on expanding local provision, particularly for SLCN, ASD, SEMH, and complex needs.

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Annex A - The Local SEND Reform Plan
findings.headline: Partnership targets £12.52m reduction in high needs spending by 2029/30, with additional £1.67m savings in SEN transport
findings.detail: The reform plan projects total cost reductions of £14.19m by 2029/30 through moderated EHCP growth, reduced independent placement reliance, and expanded local capacity. The timeline extends to 2029/30 with growth expected to slow from 2028 onwards. Success is contingent on delivering the Experts at Hand early intervention model and expanding local specialist provision.
findings.matters: High needs deficits are a material pressure for many councils; a savings plan of this scale with a specific timeline and CFO sign-off is directly relevant to peers assessing fiscal sustainability and to lenders evaluating medium-term budget risk.
findings.figures: £12.52m high needs cost reduction by 2029/30; £1.67m SEN transport reduction by 2029/30; total £14.19m target
findings.quote: The partnership anticipates a total High Needs budget cost reduction of £12.52m by 2029/30 (see Data table 1 and Assumptions) and a £1.67m reduced expenditure on SEN Transport by 2029/30

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: School place planning adjusted to deliver SEN provision through satellite sites in existing schools rather than new special school.
findings.detail: The council is delivering 152 SEN places through satellite sites in existing schools rather than building the planned Redwood Academy special school. The first provision is scheduled to open in 2027. This represents an adaptation in capital strategy to meet statutory place sufficiency requirements.
findings.matters: Capital scheme changes affect council spending plans and debt requirements; a shift from new build to satellite sites typically reduces capital cost and ongoing revenue commitments.
findings.figures: 152 SEN places; first satellite site opening 2027.
findings.quote: Deliver 152 places that would have been provided through Redwood Academy SEN special school through the delivery of SEN satellite sites of existing schools. First provision to open by 2027.

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: NHS restructuring creates risk of unfunded service transfer if areas shift to public health without budget.
findings.detail: The restructuring of NHS England includes 50% cuts to Integrated Care Boards and cuts to UKHSA. The council notes that some safeguarding and infection control functions may be cut, and some areas may shift to public health without accompanying budget. The council is engaged to understand implications and retain key staff.
findings.matters: Unfunded service transfers increase council cost pressures; a 50% ICB cut and potential service shift without funding is material downside risk for social care and public health funding.
findings.figures: 50% cuts to Integrated Care Board; cuts to UKHSA; potential unfunded service shift.
findings.quote: Possible consequential shift of some areas to public health without the budget

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: SEND transport transformation successfully reduced vehicle numbers and daily costs through tendering.
findings.detail: The council implemented transformation options approved by Portfolio Holder and Executive to reduce demand for travel assistance through revised policy and independent travel training. A tendering exercise based on optimised routes successfully reduced the number of vehicles operating and average daily costs. Work is underway to procure a new framework contract commencing September 2027.
findings.matters: SEND transport is a high-cost demand-led service; successful cost management demonstrates the council's ability to control spending pressures through service transformation.
findings.figures: Vehicle numbers reduced; average daily costs reduced; framework contract commencing September 2027.
findings.quote: The tendering exercise based on the optimised routes has been successfully delivered reducing the numbers of vehicles operating and reducing the average daily costs of routes.

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: DSG Deficit Recovery Plan agreed and being considered for 2025/26 MTFS.
findings.detail: The council has agreed principles for a Dedicated Schools Grant Deficit Recovery Plan with SEND Governance Board and Schools Forum, with the detailed plan being considered for the 2025/26 Medium Term Financial Strategy. This addresses structural underfunding affecting education and high-needs services, where 80% of Children's Services operations are demand-led and subject to cost volatility from complex placements and rising demand.
findings.matters: DSG deficits are a material pressure for councils nationally; the council's recovery plan is a critical tool for managing medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 80% of Children's Services operations are demand-led; gross risk rated 5×5=25, current 4×5=20.
findings.quote: DSG Deficit Recovery Plan principles agreed by SEND Governance Board and Schools Forum. Detailed Plan being considered as part of 2025/26 MTFS.

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: CEF Digital Transformation Programme reported slightly delayed but on track to complete within current financial year
findings.detail: The first part of the digital children's programme has gone live; discovery stage and proposed solutions identified. The programme is slightly delayed from original plan but expected to complete by end of 2026/27. Budget reduced from £121k to £115k.
findings.matters: Digital transformation delay is a relatively minor slip but indicates some project delivery challenges; completion is still forecast within the year.
findings.figures: Budget reduced from £121k to £115k; £0k actual spend in Q1
findings.quote: The Programme is slightly delayed but will be completed by the end of 26/26

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: New Childcare Places Grant projects delayed pending planning permission; no further applications planned
findings.detail: Three childcare places projects are awaiting planning permission and have been re-profiled from £373k to £218k in 2026/27. The commentary notes there are no plans in place for another round of applications, indicating a halt in pipeline development for this scheme.
findings.matters: Stalled project pipeline with no forward strategy for replacement bids suggests childcare places expansion programme may not be progressing as anticipated.
findings.figures: Budget estimate fell from £373k to £218k in 2026/27
findings.quote: Awaiting planning permission for 3 other projects. There are no plans in place for another round applications.

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Significant £6.7m rephasing out of current year reflects revised delivery timescales across multiple schemes
findings.detail: As part of Q1 monitoring, £7.556m has been moved from 2026/27 and 2028/29 into future financial years to reflect revised estimates of delivery timing. The net effect is £6.721m out of 2026/27, distributed across 2027/28 (£3.482m), 2029/30 (£4.074m), and other years. Current year budget fell from £19.5m (pre-Q1) to £12.9m (post-Q1).
findings.matters: Rephasing indicates slippage in project delivery timescales; councils and lenders monitor spend profiles to assess delivery risk and whether schemes are on track.
findings.figures: £7,556k rephased; £6,721k net from 2026/27; 2026/27 budget reduced from £19,540k to £12,855k
findings.quote: A total of £7,556k has been re-phased from 2026/27 and 2028/29 into future financial years to reflect revised estimates of when expenditure is likely to be incurred.

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: £6.8m in additional Basic Need education capital funding granted and added to the revised programme for 2030/31
findings.detail: The council has received supplementary capital funding in support of its Education Capital Programme. This new grant funding of £6.852m for Basic Need (school places) is being added to the capital programme and pushed into 2030/31. Combined with £39k Devolved Formula Capital added in Q1, the total new funding approved is £6.891k.
findings.matters: New funding awarded is a positive indicator of the council's financial position and education infrastructure priorities; it increases total available resources for the CEF portfolio from £54.8m to £61.7m.
findings.figures: Basic Need grant £6,852k; Devolved Formula Capital £39k; total new funding £6,891k
findings.quote: Subject to Executive approval, additional grant of £6,852k is requested to be incorporated into the existing capital scheme. This fund represents supplementary capital funding awarded to the Council in support of its Education Capital Programme.

findings.committee: Children, Education and Families Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Planning delays pushing back construction on multiple Operational Property Review schemes in the current year
findings.detail: Castlecombe Children's Centre, Blenheim Centre, and Adult Education schemes are all affected by planning delays that have deferred tender and construction work. The delays are pushing schemes out of the current financial year, contributing to a £6.7m rephasing out of 2026/27 to future years. OPR schemes as a whole were budgeted at £4.4m but are now estimated at £4.1m in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Planning delays create delivery risk and timing uncertainty; councils and lenders need visibility of whether capital projects will deliver as planned or slip into future years.
findings.figures: OPR schemes budget £4,408k Feb 2026 vs £4,082k Q1 estimate; £6,721k rephased from 2026/27 to future years
findings.quote: Delays in planning process for Castlecombe have pushed the construction programme out. Similarly delays with planning and design works for Blenheim have delayed the tender and subsequent works on site.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Increased proportion of waste directed to energy from waste facilities generated cost savings
findings.detail: Veolia optimised waste disposal routing in 2025/26 by directing greater volumes to energy from waste facilities rather than refuse-derived fuel outlets. This portfolio shift in disposal outlets delivered measurable cost savings for the council.
findings.matters: Shows active supply chain optimization by contractor and responsiveness to cost management, relevant to council finance officers monitoring contractor performance against value-for-money expectations.
findings.figures: Savings amount not quantified in paper
findings.quote: In 2025/26, a greater proportion was sent to energy from waste facilities than to refuse-derived fuel outlets compared with previous years, resulting in a cost saving for the Council.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Contract recycling rate above 44% threshold achieved for third time, triggering 50/50 savings share with contractor
findings.detail: The contract contains an incentive mechanism whereby savings from recycling rates above 44% are split equally between council and Veolia. This threshold has been achieved three times since the contract commenced in 2019, indicating consistent delivery above baseline performance.
findings.matters: Demonstrates council receiving additional income through performance-based incentives and contract delivering value above minimum thresholds, of interest to peer finance officers evaluating similar waste contracts.
findings.figures: 50/50 savings split, triggered three times since contract start
findings.quote: The contract contains an incentive payment whereby any savings achieved as a result of the recycling rate increasing above 44% will be shared 50/50 between the Council and Veolia.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Waste services 2025/26 outturn was £295k overspend on £24.7m budget
findings.detail: The final year outturn for combined waste and street cleaning was reported to committee in June 2026 as £295k over budget, a 1.2% variance on a £24.7m annual budget. Despite this variance, contract performance is rated as satisfactory with performance targets being met or exceeded across all three contracts.
findings.matters: Finance directors monitor budget variances in major services to understand whether cost pressures are structural, one-off, or trend-based, particularly in outsourced waste services which face volatile commodity and gate fee markets.
findings.figures: £295k overspend on £24.7m budget (1.2% variance)
findings.quote: The final 2025/26 outturn position for Waste Services was reported to this Committee on 17th June 2026, was an overspend of £295k on a total service budget for the year of £24.7m across Waste and Street Cleaning.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Waste disposal on budget in Q1 but flagged as volatile and prone to economic fluctuations.
findings.detail: Waste disposal costs are projected to be in line with budget at this stage. However, the council identifies waste tonnage as a volatile and uncertain service area prone to fluctuations depending on economic conditions. Officers will continue close monitoring.
findings.matters: Waste is inherently volatile; a council explicitly flagging and monitoring this volatility signals disciplined financial management and helps lenders track a key variable cost risk.
findings.figures: In line with budgeted expectations (variance not quantified)
findings.quote: Waste disposal costs are projected to be in line with budgeted expectations at this stage. However, waste tonnage is a potentially volatile and uncertain service area and prone to fluctuations in the economy.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Parking income shows downward trend unlikely to return to budget, requiring future budget reset.
findings.detail: The council reports a downward trend in vehicles using council car parks, reflecting national trends. While not yet showing as a budget pressure in Q1, the council states that the longer-term trend means income is unlikely to return to budgeted levels and future budget setting should account for this. The decline is attributed partly to increased compliance on traffic enforcement and bus lane cameras.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to recognise when income trends are structural rather than cyclical; this council is signalling that parking revenue should not be assumed to recover to historical budgeted levels in forward planning.
findings.figures: Downward trend (unquantified); no current budget pressure shown
findings.quote: The longer-term trend means that income is unlikely to return to budgeted levels and future budget setting should take account of this.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Highways maintenance mitigation at risk due to infrastructure age and legal obligations limiting the ability to constrain spending.
findings.detail: Officers propose mitigating the highways income shortfall through restricting infrastructure repairs to only highest-risk and essential issues. However, the council explicitly notes that infrastructure age and legal responsibilities place the ability to mitigate effectively at risk, signalling that maintenance demand cannot be indefinitely constrained without creating legal or safety exposure.
findings.matters: Finance directors tracking peers need to understand if other councils face similar tensions between budget constraints and non-negotiable infrastructure maintenance obligations driven by aging asset bases.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: However, the age of infrastructure and then need to meet our legal responsibilities, places the ability to mitigate effectively at risk.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Highways NRSWA income underachieving due to increased utility company compliance reducing road disruption.
findings.detail: Highways budget pressure is driven by NRSWA fee income falling below budget, caused by greater compliance by utility companies with regulations, which has reduced road disruption and work activity. This represents a structural change in income rather than a temporary shortfall. The council plans mitigation through restricting infrastructure repairs to high-risk and essential issues only.
findings.matters: Finance directors track how behaviour changes in other sectors create income volatility for councils; utility sector compliance is a specific mechanism that likely affects multiple councils.
findings.figures: NRSWA fees underachieving (amount unquantified)
findings.quote: The pressure on the highways budget this year is predominantly down to underachieving income budgets across various NRSWA fees, these are due to greater compliance by utility companies and therefore a reduction is road disruption and closures.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Arboriculture service projected to overspend in first quarter from essential tree management demand.
findings.detail: The Environment service shows a small budget pressure, predominantly in Arboriculture and Highways. Arboriculture works are driven by triennial inspection and reactive programmes under the adopted Tree Management Strategy to discharge statutory responsibilities and manage health and safety risks. The paper reports a projected overspend as demand for essential services exceeds budget, with review planned for Q2.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to track whether essential statutory service demands for public safety will outrun budgets and how councils manage these obligations during financial constraint.
findings.figures: Small budget pressure (unquantified)
findings.quote: Whilst there are controls in place to avoid non-essential spend, the demand for essential services will result in a projected overspend, which will be reviewed again for Q2.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Environment & Community Services Portfolio projects £410k overspend at Q1 2026/27
findings.detail: The portfolio (total budget £46.4m) is forecast to overspend by £410k by year-end based on Q1 activity—representing 1.3% of controllable budgets of £31,601k. This emerges early in the financial year against a backdrop already flagged in the council's council tax report as involving financial pressures, with the council emphasising the need for strict budgetary control to minimise risk of compounding pressures in future years.
findings.matters: Early-year overspends can compound if underlying causes persist; early identification is essential in a council already under budget pressure and flagged for financial constraints.
findings.figures: £410k overspend on controllable budget of £31,601k latest approved (1.3% variance)
findings.quote: Overall, an overspend of £410k is projected to the year-end based on the information available for the first quarter of the year.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Highways service projects £240k overspend due to underachieving NRSWA income as utility company roadwork activity declines
findings.detail: The highways service is forecasting a £240k overspend driven by underperformance across NRSWA income streams. The paper attributes this to utility companies significantly reducing roadwork activity, which affects multiple income sources: defect compliance, permit income, utility inspections, and temporary traffic regulation orders. The service will monitor activity closely throughout the year to minimise further loss.
findings.matters: External demand shocks affecting specific income streams can signal structural changes in revenues that may persist, affecting the council's financial capacity independent of its own spending control.
findings.figures: £240k overspend on Highways (latest approved budget £7,206k, projected £7,446k)
findings.quote: This variance is predominantly due to underachieving income targets across NRSWA income streams. This is due to activity being much lower than in the past, with utility companies reducing roadwork activity.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Beaverwood Depot Improvement Works completed at £20k against budget of £100k, delivering 80% cost saving
findings.detail: The Beaverwood Depot Improvement Works were completed during summer 2025 significantly under budget. Works involved welfare facility improvements including toilet block refurbishment and replacement. The £80k underspend (80% below budget) was returned to the capital programme, releasing resources for other priorities.
findings.matters: Significant underspend on a capital project demonstrates effective cost management and either prudent budgeting or efficient delivery; either way it releases capital resources that can be redeployed elsewhere in the programme.
findings.figures: Budget £100k; actual cost £20k; underspend £80k
findings.quote: The works required were significantly under the budget earmarked and were delivered for £20k, with the underspend returned to the capital programme as an underspend.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Hoblingwell Playground Project delivered at £94,941 against budget of £94,981, completed on schedule September-October 2025
findings.detail: The Hoblingwell Playground Project was completed in September-October 2025 with a £40 underspend (0.04% variance). Works included playground equipment, safety surfacing, accessibility improvements and biodiversity features. Funding comprised £74,981 from Veolia Environmental Trust and £20,000 from National Lottery Awards for All, demonstrating the council's ability to leverage external grant funding.
findings.matters: On-budget delivery of an externally-funded capital project demonstrates the council's project management capability and provides a positive counterpoint to cost pressures on other schemes in the programme.
findings.figures: Budget £94,981; actual cost £94,941.39; underspend £40
findings.quote: The project was delivered in September and October 2025 in line with the programme submitted to the grant funders and was completed at a total cost of £94,941.39.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Keston Ponds Project secured additional £363k from GLA Green Routes funding, enabling works to commence Autumn 2026
findings.detail: The council has secured an additional £363k grant funding from GLA Green Routes for the Keston Ponds Project beyond previously approved budgets, increasing the total scheme to £612k. Capital works are forecast to begin on site in Autumn 2026, with £180k of the additional funding expected to be drawn in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Successful grant funding reduces reliance on borrowing and demonstrates the council's capacity to attract external capital funding, improving financial flexibility and reducing debt burden.
findings.figures: Additional grant funding £363k; total scheme £612k; funded via GLA Green Routes
findings.quote: Additional £363k from the GLA Green Routes now secured and added to the Capital Programme. Works to start on site in Autumn 26.

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Environment and Community Services capital programme increased by £7.475m to £43.76m following Q1 monitoring revision
findings.detail: The portfolio capital programme grew from £36.285m (approved February 2026) to £43.76m following Q1 review, driven by the Depot Improvement Works borrowing request (£4.944m), TFL scheme re-alignment (£1.979m), Keston Ponds additional GLA funding (£364k), Highway Structures grant (£108k) and Gul-E EV channels grant (£89k). The single largest component of the increase is borrowing for cost overruns rather than new initiatives.
findings.matters: Material mid-year expansion of the capital programme indicates initial budget forecasts were incomplete and signals the council may face further in-year revisions; lenders track budget accuracy as an indicator of financial planning capability.
findings.figures: Revised programme £43,760k from £36,285k; net increase £7,475k
findings.quote: Revised ECS capital programme 15,033 13,587 7,204 7,171 765 43,760

findings.committee: Environment and Community Services Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council seeking £4.944m increase in external borrowing for Depot Improvement Works due to latent site conditions and contractor loss and expense claims
findings.detail: The Depot Improvement Works project is experiencing cost pressures beyond original contingencies. Latent site conditions have extended the spend profile and generated contractor claims. The council is requesting Executive approval to increase borrowing by £4.944m to fund these additional costs. The scheme total has grown from £15.028m to approximately £19.972m.
findings.matters: Mid-year borrowing requests for cost overruns on major capital projects signal cost control challenges and increase the council's debt burden; lenders assess whether projects are delivering value and staying within agreed budgets.
findings.figures: £4.944m additional borrowing; original scheme estimate £15,028k; latent conditions and contractor claims driving increase
findings.quote: There is an anticipated increased budget on this project, due to increased costs absorbing beyond original contingencies (construction and consultancy) requiring new contingency allocation due to ongoing risk and risk allocation for loss and expense claims by the contractor.

findings.committee: Renewal, Recreation and Housing Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Section 106 affordable housing agreements risk removed from register as controls now effective
findings.detail: Risk 25 has been downgraded from 3×3=9 (gross) to 1×1=1 (current) and is being removed from future risk registers. The council states controls have been implemented and are working effectively, representing improvement in financial control over developer contributions for affordable housing and supporting infrastructure.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council's ability to fix identified control weaknesses and improve development financial management
findings.figures: Risk reduced from 3×3=9 to 1×1=1. Removed from register as no longer deemed material.
findings.quote: Controls have been implemented and working effectively. The risk exists however given the control effectiveness it is no longer deemed to be a material risk and can be removed from being flagged in this risk register going forward.

findings.committee: Renewal, Recreation and Housing Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Statutory property compliance review and lift inspection contract transition both carry potential budget pressures
findings.detail: Risk 16: A statutory compliance audit running April–December 2026 will clarify landlord/tenant responsibilities for the 'big 6' compliance areas (water, electrics, gas, fire, lifts, asbestos); outcomes may reveal material budget impact. Risk 17: The LOLER lift inspection contract expires May 2027 and transfers to FM without resource handover; risk that the new contract cost will exceed current budget.
findings.matters: These represent either unknown or emerging statutory compliance cost liabilities that could impact both capital and revenue budgets
findings.figures: Compliance review runs April–December 2026. Lift contract expires May 2027. Risk 16 and 17 both rated 3×4=12.
findings.quote: Once project is complete the quantum of remedials required as well as budgetary impact (both revenue and capital) will be fully understood and which may cause budget pressure growth that will be unavoidable due to statutory nature of compliance

findings.committee: Renewal, Recreation and Housing Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Operational Property Repair programme risks budget overrun and timeline slippage from persistent building cost inflation
findings.detail: Risk 13 identifies the multi-year OPR programme—which addresses essential repairs across council property portfolio—is at material risk of exceeding budget and missing delivery timelines. Building cost inflation is ongoing and the scope of works required may exceed available budget. The council has added programme management and initiated value management, but gross risk remains high.
findings.matters: A major multi-year capital programme at material risk of cost and schedule overrun is material to budgeting and delivery credibility
findings.figures: Risk rated gross 5×4=20 (high), current 4×3=12 after mitigation. Scope and costs continue under review.
findings.quote: That building cost inflation and other economic uncertainties continue; The scope of works required exceeds the budget

findings.committee: Renewal, Recreation and Housing Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Housing scheme delivery is progressing with some completions achieved but ongoing programme risks remain
findings.detail: Risk 20 identifies housing schemes as integral to the Housing Transformation Board programme's revenue savings targets. Positive progress: West Wickham and York Rise developments are complete and let; Bellegrove and Bromley North under construction. Planning stage schemes include Castlecombe and Poverest. Manorfields TA scheme due May 2026. LAHF and CHAP funding secured. Risks persist around planning approval, inflation, and contractor performance.
findings.matters: Housing scheme delivery is tied to both statutory housing obligations and expected revenue savings targets in the transformation programme; progress and slippage both matter

findings.headline: Homelessness demand is outpacing the council's ability to contain costs within budget
findings.detail: Risk 3 identifies rising homelessness driven by structural factors—housing shortage, high rental costs, welfare cuts, evictions, and cost of living pressures—with effects that include increased out-of-borough placements and longer stays in temporary accommodation due to constrained move-on. The paper explicitly states costs cannot be contained.
findings.matters: This represents a statutory obligation under growing financial pressure with no clear resolution, a material concern for finance directors and lenders

findings.committee: Renewal, Recreation and Housing Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation cost escalation is outpacing recoverable income
findings.detail: Risk 1 identifies that temporary accommodation costs are rising due to high demand and inflation, but income recovery is not keeping pace. This creates a persistent budget imbalance in a service that should be largely recovery-based. The council explicitly names this as a key cause of housing financial strategy failure.
findings.matters: This is a statutory service with inherent demand volatility and constrained recovery, creating structural budget pressure that finance directors elsewhere would recognize as hard to solve
findings.figures: Risk rated gross 5×5=25, current 3×4=12. Despite mitigation, the service remains under material pressure.

findings.committee: Renewal, Recreation and Housing Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Capital programme funding gap risks requiring additional borrowing or reserves drawdown to proceed
findings.detail: Risk 12 identifies a potential significant shortfall in capital programme funding due to inflation, supply chain costs, property price uncertainty, and requirement to fund new housing schemes. If funding cannot be found through savings or additional income, the council would face a choice between increasing external borrowing (with MRP and interest costs falling on revenue) or drawing down already-constrained earmarked reserves. Either path increases the council's revenue budget pressure.
findings.matters: Capital funding gaps directly determine borrowing requirements and the council's financial sustainability; a key concern for any lender
findings.figures: Risk 12 gross rating 4×4=16; current rating (likelihood 2, impact 5) = 10. Impact remains unchanged at 5 despite mitigation efforts.
findings.quote: Without alternative funding, the Council would require drawdown from revenue resources. This would increase the Council's revenue budget gap and/or further deplete earmarked reserves.

Includes targeted move-on from costly placements, increased private rented sector access, and rate negotiation. The council notes that sustaining these reductions requires redirecting Homelessness Prevention Grant funding from accommodation support into prevention and incentive budgets.

findings.headline: Planning fee income remains below pre-COVID levels, creating a gap between statutory service delivery costs and achievable income
findings.detail: Planning fees are set nationally and were frozen until December 2023, when they increased by approximately one-third. Inflationary uplifts are permitted from April 2025. In-year application volumes have reduced current year pressure; future fee changes may improve the position.
findings.matters: Identifies a structural revenue pressure where the council's ability to cover statutory service costs through fees is constrained by national policy controls
findings.figures: Around one-third fee increase from December 2023
findings.quote: Planning fee income has still not recovered to pre-COVID levels. This has widened the gap between the cost of delivering statutory planning services and the income that can be achieved.

findings.headline: Average cost per temporary accommodation placement increased by £6,265 annually since Q1 2023/24, from £7,650 to £13,915 per placement
findings.detail: Escalation reflects withdrawal of housing providers from temporary accommodation and the private rented market, combined with demand from other local authorities and the Home Office. Service redesign and taskforce work are reducing both placement numbers and average costs.
findings.matters: Demonstrates a structural cost escalation in a major service area that has driven overspend; evidence of management response shows cost trajectory is beginning to reverse but this represents a material liability increase since 2023/24
findings.figures: £6,265 annual increase per placement; £7,650 to £13,915
findings.quote: Since Q1 2023/24, the average weighted net cost of placements has increased by £6,265 per placement per year, from £7,650 to £13,915. However, the housing service redesign and focused taskforce work are now reducing both the number and average cost of nightly paid placements.
